claim: Visitor, host, chosen winter evening, dinner, household tasks and arrangement of one illustrative hanok are fictional framing.
limit: No named historical resident, exact house survey, documented dinner or measured temperature implied.

claim: Traditional ondol sends hot combustion gases from a firebox through under-floor passages, warming stone slabs before smoke exits a chimney.
limit: Combustion gases stay below the sealed floor; not hot water or room ventilation.

claim: A lowered kitchen hearth can combine cooking above the firebox with heating an adjoining room; stone, earth and paper form layers above flues.
locator: KOFIC construction; Bishop inn furnace passage
limit: One arrangement, not every ondol; no exact dimensions. Never put paper directly above open flames.

claim: Stone slabs act as thermal storage, retaining heat after the fire has declined; duration depends on conditions.
locator: Accessible introduction, traditional stone slab paragraph
limit: No historical thermostat reading, promised hours, modern experiment extrapolation or perpetual heat.

claim: The floor near the firebox tends to be warmer; heat distribution and channel arrangement vary.
limit: No uniform temperature map or universal hottest-seat etiquette.

claim: Floor heating is associated with sitting, eating and sleeping at floor level; outdoor shoes are generally removed; small soban tables serve floor-level dining.
locator: Floor lifestyle passages and museum education entry
limit: No disappearance of all chairs or one posture mandatory for every person.

claim: Hanok can combine a heated room with a ventilated raised wooden maru useful in summer.
limit: Maru is not heated stone flooring; no universal house plan or quantitative cooling guarantee.

claim: Bishop described brushwood entering Seoul and smoke from cooking/heating fires; fuel gathering and delivery supported household warmth.
limit: Attribute observation; no exact daily schedule, pollution statistic, fuel price or efficiency ratio.

claim: Bishop described becoming uncomfortably hot in a Korean temple cell heated by adjacent kitchen flues.
locator: Temple cell beside guests' kitchen, 91°F passage
limit: Her particular reported experience; do not transfer to Seoul household or imply normal temperature; do not narrate exact number.

claim: Bishop noted tough buff oiled paper used on floors of middle- and upper-class houses.
limit: Not every floor or class; no unsupported recipe or durability promise.

claim: Kim Chun-yeong's c.1890 Samcheong-dong house illustrates compact middle/upper-class Seoul housing; it was later moved for preservation.
limit: Not a poor family's house; no original Namsangol location or measured ondol plan.

claim: Men's traditional clothing includes jeogori, baji with ankle ties and outer coats; padded winter clothing appears in contemporary accounts.
locator: Museum men's hanbok; Bishop winter clothing p.27
limit: Visitor clothing is an understated adaptation, not a documented person's exact outfit or every local's costume.

claim: The system trades fuel and tending work for stored warmth; an intact separated combustion route is essential to the illustrated mechanism.
locator: Synthesis of construction, fuel and thermal storage
limit: Not a building manual, health guarantee, emissions comparison or numerical efficiency claim.

claim: Early partial-floor heating and later whole-floor arrangements differed; modern hydronic ondol uses pipes and is mechanically different from the illustrated hearth system.
limit: No precise universal transition date, invention race, or claim no electricity existed in Seoul c.1900.
